design_detail: Two-page Comment (The Lancet Psychiatry, published online 31 October 2019) by a former FDA medical officer, setting out seven concerns about the efficacy evidence behind the US approval of intranasal esketamine (the S-enantiomer of ketamine) for treatment-resistant depression on 5 March 2019. The evidence is the public record of the 12 February 2019 FDA advisory committee meeting (FDA briefing document, Janssen briefing document, slides and transcript), cited by page, plus the published trial reports and one meta-analysis of other drugs. The author adds his own re-analyses without stated methods: a Fisher's exact test of relapse with and without one outlier site in the relapse-prevention trial (study 3003), a pooled standardized mean difference for the three short-term phase 3 trials, and a placebo-to-drug ratio of mean MADRS change. No search strategy. The PDF read is the online-first version, paginated 1 to 2.
can_establish: What the public FDA advisory-committee documents show on the points the author selected: how treatment resistance was defined and distributed in the esketamine phase 3 trials, which trials were positive, how the relapse-prevention trial was enriched and how far its result depended on one site, and how small the reported rapid-response rates were.
cannot_establish: Whether esketamine works less well than other treatments (the comparison with other drugs is across different trials and populations), how the author's pooled effect size and sensitivity analysis were computed (no methods are given), or the evidence for esketamine's efficacy in full, since the Comment presents concerns only.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (commentary). The cited trials: three short-term phase 3 trials (3001, 3002 and 3005, the last in people aged 65 or older) that together entered 702 patients, and the randomized withdrawal trial 3003 (p. 1 of the online-first PDF).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria; the author chose the points.
sample.selection_effects: The source documents are a defined and complete public record of the phase 3 programme, which limits selection of trials; the selection of points within them is the author's and is limited to concerns.

exposure.measurement: As in the cited trials: intranasal esketamine (fixed doses of 56 mg and 84 mg are named in a quoted FDA sentence on trial 3001), combined with a newly started oral antidepressant in trials 3001 and 3002 according to the titles of their cited reports (pp. 1–2 of the online-first PDF).

comparison.controls: Placebo in the cited trials; for the author's comparison of effect sizes, published standardized mean differences for olanzapine-fluoxetine, aripiprazole and quetiapine from a separate meta-analysis (p. 2 of the online-first PDF).

outcomes.instruments: As cited: Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) change in the short-term trials; relapse in the withdrawal trial; rapid clinical response (definition not given in the Comment) (pp. 1–2 of the online-first PDF).
outcomes.operationalization: Efficacy is judged from the drug-placebo difference in mean MADRS change, the share of the drug group's change also seen with placebo, a pooled standardized mean difference, relapse proportions and rapid-response proportions.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable. The author reports his own Fisher's exact tests (three in the figure) without correction.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited from the FDA documents (pp. 1–2 of the online-first PDF): in trial 3002, mean MADRS decrease 20.8 with esketamine against 16.8 with placebo; trial 3005 (65 or older) p = 0.06; in 3003, relapse 22% printed for esketamine (n = 90) against 45% for placebo (n = 86), Fisher's exact p = 0.012; at the outlier site, 22% (n = 9) against 100% (n = 16), p = 0.0001; excluding that site, 27% against 33%, p = 0.48; rapid response in about 10% of patients given esketamine overall, and in 3002 8% against 5% with placebo (Fisher's exact p = 0.32). Author's own pooling of the three short-term trials: standardized mean difference 0.28 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.44), compared with olanzapine-fluoxetine 0.26 (0.04 to 0.45), aripiprazole 0.35 (0.23 to 0.48) and quetiapine 0.40 (0.26 to 0.53) from a published meta-analysis. Editors' calculation: 16.8 divided by 20.8 is 0.81, the basis of the author's 81%; the printed p values are reproduced exactly by relapse in 24 of 90 (27%) against 39 of 86 overall, 2 of 9 against 16 of 16 at the outlier site, and 22 of 81 against 23 of 70 elsewhere.
analysis.selective_reporting: By design the Comment reports concerns only; the sponsor's case is mentioned in one clause (the sponsor argues the 3002 difference is clinically meaningful) and the FDA's site inspection in another. Methods for the pooled effect size (which arms, which model, which SDs) and for the sensitivity analysis are not given.

interpretation_gap.results_show: From the FDA's own documents: two of the three short-term phase 3 trials were not statistically significant (one, in older adults, p = 0.06); in the positive trial the MADRS change with placebo was about four-fifths of that with esketamine; the relapse-prevention trial enrolled only people who had remitted on esketamine and its significance depended on one site where every placebo patient relapsed; most participants had failed antidepressants from one or two classes only; and rapid response was uncommon and did not differ significantly from placebo in trial 3002.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The author concludes that esketamine's novel mechanism does not appear to confer efficacy beyond that of cheaper alternatives, wonders whether the novelty encouraged regulatory leniency, and suggests clinicians and patients temper their expectations (p. 2 of the online-first PDF). The first conclusion rests on comparing a pooled effect size, computed by methods not shown, with effect sizes of other drugs from different trials in different populations (adjunctive treatment of depression), which cannot show that esketamine is no better than those drugs. The point about leniency is framed as a question. The opening paragraph announces concerns about the safety of esketamine, while all seven concerns, and the title, are about efficacy and approval.

timeline.event: Daly et al.: phase 2 trial of intranasal esketamine with continued oral antidepressants, sponsored by Janssen (this round's first-pass card sc_daly_2018).

FDA advisory committee meeting (12 February) and approval of intranasal esketamine for treatment-resistant depression (5 March), as described in this Comment; the phase 3 reports cited are Popova et al. (2019, trial 3002) and Fedgchin et al. (2019, trial 3001).
This Comment: seven concerns about the efficacy evidence and the approval.
Horowitz and Moncrieff: a critical review of the same phase 3 evidence (online first 2020), with a published corrigendum.

replication.where_it_stands: The Comment's factual points are drawn from public regulatory documents and can be checked there; its comparative conclusion is an indirect comparison. A pooled estimate of esketamine against placebo from a systematic review is on the Tier A list (Dean et al., 2021; Nikolin et al., 2023, being read by other readers in this round).

funding.funder: The author states that the work was not funded (p. 2 of the online-first PDF).
funding.declared_conflicts: The author states he has no financial interest in esketamine or competing treatments; he previously worked as an FDA medical officer reviewing drug applications, and is a current member of the FDA Psychopharmacologic Drugs Advisory Committee, which met with the Drug Safety and Risk Management Advisory Committee in February 2019 on esketamine, although he did not take part in that meeting because of the government shutdown (p. 2 of the online-first PDF).
funding.affiliations_note: Portland VA Medical Center (Behavioral Health and Neurosciences Division) and Oregon Health and Science University. The author acknowledges Peter Cary for drawing his attention to the outlier site. His standing as a former FDA reviewer and current advisory committee member is relevant to his reading of the regulatory documents. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the Comment.

what_would_settle_it: An independent re-analysis of the patient-level data of the esketamine phase 3 programme, including time to relapse in study 3003 with and without the outlier site and onset of response by a pre-specified definition; and a randomized trial comparing esketamine with an established augmentation strategy in people with more extensive treatment resistance.

domains.note: No literature search, but the source is explicit and complete for its purpose: the public regulatory record of the phase 3 programme, cited by document and page. The points chosen from it are the author's.

The Comment is itself an appraisal of the trials (definition of resistance, enrichment, dependence on one site, hierarchical testing), but it takes the comparator meta-analysis at face value and gives no methods for its own pooling and sensitivity analysis.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The evidence is the sponsor's and the FDA's; the author cites none of his own studies.

Factual points carry page references to the FDA documents; inferences (less efficacy in more resistant patients; regulatory leniency) are marked as possibilities, but the efficacy comparison with other drugs is stated as a conclusion from an indirect comparison.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against esketamine's efficacy and approval (the case for efficacy is under-represented)
domains.note: Concerns only, by design: the sponsor's and the FDA's reasons for regarding the evidence as sufficient are reduced to two clauses.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a commentary (METHODS §5.3). The Comment is short, transparent about its sources and cites them by page, which makes its factual points checkable; its weaknesses are deliberate one-sidedness, unstated methods for its own analyses, a figure with labelling errors, and a conclusion drawn from an indirect comparison. It may be cited for what the FDA documents show on the points it raises (with the document page it gives) and as a critique of the approval; numbers about the trials should, where possible, be cited to the trial reports or the FDA documents themselves, and the claim that esketamine is no more effective than cheaper alternatives may not be cited as a finding.

key_findings.finding: The phase 3 trials used a regulatory definition of treatment-resistant depression (failure of any two antidepressants); of the 702 patients who entered the three short-term phase 3 trials, 22% had failed antidepressants of just one class, 60% of two classes and 18% of three or four classes; failure of psychotherapy was not required.
key_findings.locator: 2nd paragraph (left column), citing FDA briefing document p. 15 and Janssen briefing document p. 67

key_findings.finding: Two of the three short-term phase 3 trials were not significant; one of them (study 3005, NCT02422186) enrolled people aged 65 or older (p = 0.06) and was unpublished at the time.

In the only positive short-term phase 3 trial (3002), the mean MADRS decrease from baseline was 20.8 with esketamine and 16.8 with placebo (FDA slide 24); the author calculates that 81% of the response to esketamine was also seen with placebo.
key_findings.note: Horowitz and Moncrieff (horowitz_2021, p. 2 of its online-first PDF), citing the FDA review, give 19.8 and 15.8 for the same trial; both give a 4-point difference. The trial report or the FDA documents should decide which pair is right.

key_findings.finding: The randomized withdrawal trial (3003) admitted only patients previously randomized to esketamine (not placebo) in a short-term trial who reached stable remission (FDA slides 20 and 29), an enriched population.

The FDA briefing document (p. 25) noted that one site in Poland, where every placebo patient relapsed, drove the overall result of trial 3003; the FDA told its committee, after a member's question, that its inspection found no reason to question data integrity. The author's re-analysis of the relapse proportions: significant with all sites (Fisher's exact p = 0.012), p = 0.0001 within the outlier site (esketamine n = 9, placebo n = 16), not significant without that site (p = 0.48).
key_findings.note: The figure's labels are partly wrong; see reporting issue 1. Time to relapse and the hazard ratio could not be recalculated without patient-level data, as the author states.

key_findings.finding: The author's pooling of the primary outcomes of the three short-term trials (FDA slide 24) gives a standardized mean difference of 0.28 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.44), which he compares with 0.26 (0.04 to 0.45) for olanzapine-fluoxetine and 0.35 (0.23 to 0.48) for aripiprazole and 0.40 (0.26 to 0.53) for quetiapine as adjunctive treatments, from a published meta-analysis.
key_findings.note: No methods are given for the pooling; the comparison is across different trials and populations, not head to head.

key_findings.finding: Rapid onset was not formally demonstrated: in trial 3001 the onset of clinical response could not be formally tested for the 56 mg and 84 mg doses because earlier endpoints in the testing hierarchy were not significant (Janssen briefing document p. 234); about 10% of patients given esketamine had a rapid clinical response; in trial 3002 it was 8% against 5% with placebo (Fisher's exact p = 0.32); for trial 3005 the mean changes with esketamine and placebo were essentially superimposable until day 22 (FDA slide 37).
key_findings.note: The definition of rapid clinical response is not given in the Comment; it is in the cited briefing documents.

key_findings.finding: The author asks whether esketamine's novel mechanism encouraged leniency regarding these concerns and concludes that clinicians and patients might wish to temper their expectations.

reporting_issues.issue: The figure's labels for trial 3003 do not fit its own bars and p values. The bar for esketamine at all sites is drawn at about 27% but labelled 22%, and the 'excluding outlier' bars are labelled esketamine n = 70 and placebo n = 81. Editors' calculation: the all-site and outlier-site totals (90 minus 9; 86 minus 16) give 81 for esketamine and 70 for placebo; the printed p values (0.012, 0.0001 and 0.48) are reproduced exactly by relapse in 24 of 90 (27%) against 39 of 86 overall, 2 of 9 against 16 of 16 at the outlier site, and 22 of 81 (27%) against 23 of 70 (33%) elsewhere; with 22% (20 of 90) the overall p would be about 0.001.
reporting_issues.consequence: The esketamine relapse proportion in 3003 should not be quoted from this figure as 22%; the counts must be checked against the trial report or the FDA briefing document.

reporting_issues.issue: The opening paragraph says the FDA documents reveal concerns regarding the safety of esketamine, whereas the title and all seven concerns are about efficacy and the approval decision.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the Comment should not be cited for safety concerns.

reporting_issues.issue: The pooled standardized mean difference (0.28) and the sensitivity analysis of trial 3003 are presented without methods (arms included, model, source of standard deviations; relapse counts used).
reporting_issues.consequence: These figures are the author's unreproducible calculations from summary data and should be cited as his, not as trial results.

verification.source_read: PDF PDFs/Ketamine/Turner_2019_EsketamineSevenConcerns.pdf: the online-first version (The Lancet Psychiatry, published online 31 October 2019), paginated 1–2, not the issue pagination (6(12), 977–979, per the reference record); anchors cite 'of the online-first PDF'. Read in full: text, figure and legend (rendered at 150 and 300 dpi), author note, declaration and references. The cited FDA and Janssen briefing documents were not read.
